## What a call debit spread is and how it pays
You *pay* $1.85 to own the $140 call and finance it by selling the $145 call. It's a **bullish, defined-risk, defined-reward** bet:

| XOM at Jul 31 | P&L (1 ct) |
|---|---|
| ≤ $140 | **−$185** (max loss = the debit) |
| $141.85 | $0 (breakeven) |
| $143 | +$115 |
| ≥ $145 | **+$315** (max profit) |

Key difference from the put-credit spreads you've been doing: a put-credit wins if the stock just **stays flat or up**. This **needs XOM to actually rise** past $141.85. More directional, wins less often, but a cleaner payoff when it moves.

## Why it's routed call-debit, not put-credit
This is the router fix in action. **XOM's IV is ~29% — dirt cheap.** When IV is low, options are cheap to *buy* and selling premium pays too little to be worth the risk. So the matrix says: bullish + cheap IV → **buy the move** (call debit). Contrast HPE at 69% IV → *sell* a put credit. Same "bullish," opposite structure, because IV is opposite.

1. **Sector rotation.** Money is fleeing high-beta tech (QQQ −1.3%, semis −5–9%) and hiding in **energy + defensives**. XOM +2.4%, **CVX +2.5%** — the *whole* sector is bid while tech bleeds. That's a real risk-[REDACTED] rotation, not a one-name pop.

4. **It's a haven bid** — XOM is low-beta, big dividend, defensive. On a scared tape it's where capital rotates *to*.

- **It's directional — flat = a loss.** If XOM just sits at $139.74, you lose money (theta bleeds the debit). It *must* climb to $141.85+.
- **Oil is the swing factor and it's fickle.** Today's +2.8% could be a one-day inventory/geopolitics blip. If oil reverses, XOM gives it back.
- **Rotation trades unwind fast.** If tech bounces tomorrow, the defensive-into-energy bid can reverse in a session.

- **Call-debits are low-hit-rate by nature** — the backtest showed ~39% win rate (but big winners). Don't expect a put-credit-style 75% probability.

## 460. assistant

The page itself is auth-gated (came back empty), but I know the program well — that's Robinhood's **Stock Lending**. Here's the honest read on whether it fits our setup ([robinhood.com/account/stock-lending](https://robinhood.com/account/stock-lending)).

## What it is
You opt in, and Robinhood lends your **fully-paid shares** to other market participants (mostly short sellers). You keep full market exposure — you can still sell anytime, and gains/losses stay yours — and you collect a **monthly cash payment** based on the borrow demand for your shares.

## How the income actually works
Payment ≈ `shares × price × annualized borrow rate × (your cut of the fee) ÷ 12`.

The catch is the **borrow rate**, which is demand-driven:
- **Liquid large-caps** (GOOGL, AAPL, NVDA, AVGO…): borrow rate ~**0.01–0.25%/yr**. Income is literally **pennies**.
- **Hard-to-borrow names** (heavily-shorted small-caps, low-float, meme/squeeze, some biotech, fresh IPOs): **5% to 100%+/yr** — where real money is.

## The real costs (why it's not free money)
1. **SIPC coverage drops** on shares while they're on loan. RH posts third-party cash collateral instead, but it's a weaker protection than SIPC.
2. **Dividends become "cash-in-lieu"** — taxed as **ordinary income**, not qualified dividends. You lose the favorable dividend tax rate.
3. **You lose proxy/voting rights** on lent shares.

## Verdict for our two accounts
| Account | Holding | Stock-lending fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Agentic $1k** | GOOGL 2 sh | 🔴 **Not worth it.** GOOGL borrow rate ≈ 0 → ~$0 income, and it's a name we're **actively recycling** (resting $372 sell). Adds tax/SIPC friction for pennies. |
| **Options book** | 6 put-credit **spreads** | ⚪ **N/A** — lending applies to long *shares*, not options. |

**Bottom line: skip it for what we hold now.** Our capital is in defined-risk options (not lendable) plus a tiny, fast-turning GOOGL position (near-zero borrow). Stock lending is built for **buy-and-hold portfolios sitting on hard-to-borrow names** — the opposite of our recycle/premium-selling motion.

## The one scenario where it *would* pay
If the strategy ever holds a **hard-to-borrow name as long shares** for a stretch — e.g., a heavily-shorted small-cap like **NNE** (nuclear, high short interest), a squeeze candidate, or a hot IPO — the borrow rate could be genuinely high (5–50%+), and lending would stack real yield on top of the position. Worth flagging *at that time*, sized against the SIPC/tax tradeoff.

## What the "CPI gate" is
It's a specific case of the **event gate** — the rule: **never *sell* premium (open a new credit spread) right before a scheduled binary event** (CPI, PCE, FOMC, or a stock's earnings). CPI = the June inflation report, out **tomorrow 8:30 AM ET**, one hour *before* the market opens. It's the biggest 2-way market event of the month, and this one's extra loaded (banks + Warsh testimony same morning).

## Why it blocks *new credit sells* specifically
When you sell a put credit spread, your payoff is lopsided **in your favor only in calm markets**:
- **Max gain** = the small credit you collect (e.g. $0.80).
- **Max loss** = the full width minus credit (e.g. $5 − $0.80 = $4.20).

You're risking ~$4 to make ~$0.80. That's fine when the tape drifts, because *time + probability* are on your side. But a scheduled event **widens the range of outcomes** — and worse, **the move happens as an overnight gap** (CPI hits at 8:30, market opens at 9:30). 

**You can't manage a gap.** No stop, no roll, no intraday exit — you wake up already through your short strike. So right before CPI, you'd be taking your *worst* risk/reward (tiny reward, full-width risk) at the *one moment* the odds of a big adverse gap are highest. That's the trap the gate exists to prevent.

## The "juicy premium" trap
Here's the part that fools people: **IV is elevated *into* the event**, so premiums look fat and tempting. But that's not free money — the market is *correctly pricing* the danger. You're not being overpaid; you're being paid for real risk. Then right after the print, **IV crushes**. 

So the professional sequence is the reverse of the temptation:
- ❌ **Sell into CPI** = collect inflated premium, eat the gap risk.
- ✅ **Sell *after* CPI** = the uncertainty is resolved, IV collapses, and you harvest that crush on a *confirmed* direction.

That's why I want to wait one day, not because energy or NBIS aren't attractive — they are — but because Wednesday's entry is structurally better than Monday's.

## What's actually "blocked" vs still allowed
The gate is narrow — it only blocks **new short-premium** trades. It does **not** block:

| Action | Blocked by CPI gate? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Open a new **put/call credit spread** (sell premium) | 🔴 **Yes** | full-width gap risk for tiny reward |
| **Close NNE** (buy-to-close) | 🟢 No | *reduces* risk — always allowed |
| **Trim/roll AVGO** to de-risk | 🟢 No | risk-[REDACTED] |
| A **defined-risk debit** (call/put debit spread) | 🟡 Allowed | max loss = the small debit you paid; a gap can't cost more than that |
| Buying **shares** in the $1k sleeve | 🟡 Allowed | your choice, just size it |

## Concrete example on your book
Say you sold a fresh NBIS $205/$195 put credit today for ~$1.00 into the $209 dip. If June CPI runs **hot** tomorrow (core ≥0.3%), growth/AI names gap down — NBIS could open $190. You'd be **max loss (−$900 on that spread) at the open with no chance to react**, all to have collected $100. That single gap erases a week of green closes — the exact "one forced max-loss" the learning log warns about.

Versus: wait for the print. If CPI cools and NBIS *holds* $205–210 Wednesday, you sell the same spread into a **confirmed** hold with IV crushing in your favor. Same trade, dramatically better odds.

**So the gate isn't "don't trade" — it's "don't sell premium blind into a coin-flip you can't manage."** Today you close NNE (allowed, risk-[REDACTED]) and optionally de-risk AVGO; tomorrow you watch the print; Wednesday you deploy. Want me to price the **AVGO de-risk** now, or set the exact **post-CPI triggers** for NBIS/energy so they're ready to fire Wednesday?

The core issue is asymmetry: when you sell a put credit spread, you pocket a small premium but risk the full width if the stock gaps through your short strike overnight on a hot CPI print. IV is artificially elevated into the event (making premiums look attractive), but that's the market correctly pricing real binary risk, not overpaying you. After the event, IV crushes—which is why you want to *sell* premium *after* the data, not before. The "block" doesn't prevent all trades, just new short premium positions; defined-risk debit spreads can still trade through the gate. ## 805. assistant

Good question — "rolling" is a specific options move, and it matters for the NNE decision. Here's what it means, using your actual position.

## What "rolling" is
Rolling = **closing your current spread and opening a new one further out in time (and sometimes at different strikes), in a single trade.** You're not exiting the trade — you're *extending* it, buying yourself more time for NNE to recover.

## Your NNE situation
You're short the **$23/$20 put credit spread ×5, expiring Friday 7/17**, with NNE at ~$17.58 — deep in the money. If it expires there, you eat close to the full **~$1,100 max loss**.

You have two choices Thursday:

**Option A — Close (take the L)**
- Buy the spread back now, lock in the loss (~$1,100-ish), free the collateral, walk away.
- Clean. Done. Move the money to better trades.

**Option B — Roll (extend the bet)**
- Simultaneously: **buy back** the 7/17 spread (closing it) **and sell** a new NNE spread expiring later — say Aug or Sept.
- The longer-dated spread you sell brings in **more premium** than the near-dated one costs to close → you often collect a **net credit** for rolling.
- That credit **reduces your effective loss** and gives NNE weeks longer to climb back above $20/$23.

## The catch (why it's not automatic)
Rolling is **not** a free save — it's *adding time and risk to a losing trade*:
- You're keeping ~$1,100+ of capital tied up and at risk for another month+.
- If NNE keeps falling, you lose on the roll *too* — you've just delayed and possibly enlarged the loss.
- The old trading sin is "rolling a loser to avoid admitting it" — throwing good money after bad.

**The decision rule:** roll only if the math genuinely beats closing — i.e., the net credit is meaningful *and* you have a real reason to believe NNE recovers (base rate, catalyst). Otherwise, closing is the disciplined move.

## Simple analogy
- **Close** = fold the hand, take your loss, keep the rest of your chips.
- **Roll** = double-down for another round — only worth it if the odds actually favor you, not just to avoid folding.

Tomorrow I'll pull the live numbers and show you *exactly* what credit a roll to August would bring in vs. the cost to close — so it's a math decision, not a hope decision. My lean, honestly: NNE's been a slow bleed for weeks, so unless the roll credit is unusually rich, **closing is probably the cleaner call**. But I'll show you both before you decide.

## GS buy-to-close GTC — the mechanics

**What you placed:** buy back the $1050/$1040 spread ×2 at a **$0.40 net debit**, GTC.

- You sold it for **$0.90**. Buying it back at **$0.40** locks **+$0.50/spread × 2 × 100 = +$100** (~56% of max).
- Current closing cost is ~**$0.80** (bid), so your $0.40 sits **below market** — it's a resting take-profit that fills only as the spread decays toward $0.40 (GS holding/rising + theta).
- **The nice part:** if it never fills but GS stays >$1,050 into 7/31, the spread expires worthless and you keep the **full $180 credit** anyway. So this order is pure upside — early harvest or full credit, no downside to having it in.

## 1117. assistant

**No — that $1,000 scenario doesn’t happen on this trade.**

Assignment on a **short put** only happens when XE is **below $12.50** (put is ITM). At **$17.50**, the $12.50 put is **$5 OTM** — nobody exercises it, so you are **not** handed 200 shares.

### What actually happens at each price

| XE at expiry | Assignment? | Your result |
|---|---|---|
| **$17.50** (where it is now) | **No** | Puts expire worthless → keep credit **+$130** only |
| **$12.50** exactly | Borderline / usually no | Still ~**+$130** |
| **Below $12.50** (e.g. $10) | **Yes** — you buy 200 @ $12.50 | You’re **buying the dip**, not capturing a $17→$12 gain |

### Why the $1,000 math is backwards
`($17.50 − $12.50) × 200 = $1,000` would only apply if you **already owned** shares bought at $12.50 and sold at $17.50.

As the **put seller**, you only get shares when the stock has **fallen** under $12.50 — so your mark would look like:

- Assigned @ $12.50, XE at $10 → **unrealized loss**, not a gain  
- Net basis after credit ≈ **$11.85** → still red until XE climbs back above that

### Bottom line
At **$17.17–$17.50**, holding = racing for the last **~$46** to turn +$84 into +$130. You do **not** get a free $1,000 share windfall from assignment at these prices.

Yes — **because these are puts, not calls.**

| You sold | Assignment means | Happens when |
|---|---|---|
| **Put** (what you have) | You’re **forced to buy** 200 shares @ $12.50 | Stock is **below** $12.50 |
| **Call** | You’re **forced to sell** 200 shares @ strike | Stock is **above** the strike |

So with short puts:
- Stock **up** at $17.50 → puts die worthless → you keep the **$130** credit. No shares.
- Stock **down** under $12.50 → you get shares at $12.50 (a falling knife), not a $17 lottery ticket.

The “buy low / stock rips to $17” story only works if you **chose** to buy shares (or got assigned on a put when it was weak and then it recovered). It doesn’t come from assignment while XE is already at $17.

IBD Big Cap 20
Howmet Stock Pops After Earnings But Remains Inside Buy Zone
FacebookXLinkedInShare Licensing
RACHEL FOX11:32 AM ET 08/07/2026
Howmet (HWM) is the Big Cap 20 component in focus as the stock tests a key level after breaking out in June. The stock is wading in a 5% buy zone, rendering it actionable now.

A handful of aerospace and defense stocks gained momentum on Thursday. Both Howmet and fellow aerospace stock ATI (ATI) reported robust earnings, causing several of these names to rally in unison.

How To Buy Stocks: Flat Base Chart Pattern
See All Videos
Howmet stock has a Composite Rating of 98, bolstered by recent consistency in earnings and sales growth stemming partially from the artificial intelligence boom. The Pittsburgh-based company is a major supplier of jet engine components, aerospace fasteners, and airframe structural components for commercial and military aircraft.

The company's second-quarter results vaulted over Wall Street's targets. Adjusted earnings jumped 46% to $1.33 per share, beating expectations of $1.24. Revenue surged 24% to $2.55 billion, above expectations of $2.43 billion. Noting stronger demand for electricity generation, "especially from natural gas for data centers," Howmet said on its earnings call that sales for gas turbines popped 38%.

Also, Howmet delivered a better-than-expected outlook for its third quarter and hiked its 2026 view. The components maker expects third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36 on $2.565 billion to $2.585 billion in revenue. Wall Street had anticipated $1.26 per share on $2.47 billion in revenue.

Howmet Trading Inside A Buy Zone
Howmet has soared 43% so far in 2026. The stock has been a steady climber with multiple pullbacks to the 50-day moving average. Recent breakouts have failed to yield a 20% to 25% gain from the buy point. But shares continue to step higher.

The stock has been trading sideways inside the 5% buy zone from a five-week flat base. The buy point is at 280.74 and the buy zone extends to 294.77. Shares briefly became extended from this area intraday on Thursday amid the morning rally. But the stock has since pared early gains and returned to the buy zone.

Earnings growth has revved up in recent quarters, from 42% to 46%. Sales growth has also gained traction, from 19% to 24%.

Two AI Names Bounce From Chip Sell-Off; Three More IBD 50 Stocks On Watch

VIDYA RAMAKRISHNAN11:11 AM ET 08/07/2026
After a sell-off in chip stocks in July, a few artificial intelligence infrastructure names in the IBD 50 are recovering. Teradyne (TER) and Credo Technology (CRDO) are setting up in bases in the stock market.

Three other IBD 50 stocks near buy points include a network storage provider, a copper play and an insurance underwriter.

↑X
NOW PLAYING
What Stocks Should You Be Buying? Try Mike Webster's Weekend Watchlist Routine To Find Out
Teradyne (TER) has retaken its 10-week moving average after shares triggered a sell signal from a buy point at 422.11. The stock found support at its 40-week line and is forming a cup base with a potential 487.91 buy point.

Teradyne provides automated testing for NAND and DRAM memory chips and robotic systems. The company is benefiting from a bottleneck for AI infrastructure that has sent memory prices soaring.

For the second quarter, revenue from memory testing hit a record, while earnings of $2.47 per share topped Wall Street's expectations of $2.09. Total revenue of $1.33 billion more than doubled from the prior year, and came in well above estimates of $1.22 billion.

The company guided $2 in third-quarter earnings per share and $1.25 billion in sales at the midpoint. That was above FactSet estimates of $1.56 in EPS and $1.06 billion in sales.

The stock holds a top EPS Rating of 99 and a Composite Rating of 94. Shares have outperformed 92% of other stocks Investor's Business Daily tracks over the past 52 weeks.

Credo Technology Beats Estimates
Credo Technology Group (CRDO) is forming a cup base that offers an entry at 308.67. This is a late-stage base that may not net the higher gains that early-stage ones do. It has a higher chance of failing, too.

Credo provides copper and optical interconnect solutions used in data centers. The stock holds a Relative Strength Rating of 94.

See The Latest Updates To IBD Watchlists

Fourth-quarter earnings of $1.16 per share on sales of $437 million beat estimates of $1.02 and $432 million, respectively.

Profit estimates for 2026 suggest a 144% increase to $6.12 per share. For 2027, analysts are targeting 48% growth, or $9.04.

Skyward Specialty Insurance (SKWD) is in a buy zone. Shares broke out July 28 from a cup-with-handle base with an entry at 63.03. The buy zone goes to 66.18.

The company topped Wall Street's target of a 31% increase in second-quarter earnings. Earnings climbed 46% year over year to $1.30 per share. Gross written premiums rose 13% to $741 million.

Skyward provides specialty and casualty insurance services in the U.S. and the U.K. Analysts polled by FactSet have raised their full-year profit estimates 24% to $4.95 per share. For 2027, earnings estimates of $5.52 per share point to 11% growth.

Skyward Specialty is also an IBD Sector Leader and heads the insurance sector, one of Investor's Business Daily's 30 sectors.

Stock Market: Copper Stock In Early Base
Southern Copper (SCCO) continues to form a long base with an entry at 221.67.

Accelerating earnings growth over the four most recent quarters has helped the stock score an EPS Rating of 98, while its all-around performance places the stock among the top 4% of all stocks tracked by IBD.

Also a related AI name, NetApp (NTAP) is trying to break out above a 192.83 buy point from a cup base. The buy point is also the stock's all-time high.

<timestamp>Tuesday, Aug 11, 2026, 8:15 AM (UTC-7)</timestamp>

explain me the risk, whats short strike

## 1348. assistant

### What “short strike” means

On a **put credit spread** you do two things:

1. **Sell (short) a put** — this is the **short strike** (the higher strike)
2. **Buy (long) a put** — this is the **long strike** (the lower strike, your insurance)

Example HOOD **90/85**:
- **Short strike = $90** → you sold the Sep 18 $90 put  
- **Long strike = $85** → you bought the Sep 18 $85 put  

You collected a credit for selling that package. You win if HOOD stays **above the short strike** at expiration (or you close earlier for less than you collected).

---

### How the risk works

Think of the short put as: *“I agree I may have to buy 100 shares at the short strike.”*  
The long put caps how bad that can get.

| HOOD at expiry | What happens (90/85) |
|---|---|
| **Above $90** | Both puts expire worthless → you keep full credit (~$190) |
| **Between $90 and $85** | Short put is ITM → losses grow; long put still helps a bit |
| **At / below $85** | **Max loss** hit → width − credit = $5 − $1.90 ≈ **$310** per contract |

**Breakeven** = short strike − credit  
- 90/85 @ $1.90 → BE **$88.10**  
- Below BE you lose; above BE (at expiry) you profit

**Max loss** is never the full stock price — only the **$5 width** minus credit, because the long put stops further damage.

---

### Why short strike matters most

The **short strike is the danger line**.

- Distance from spot to short strike = your **cushion**
- Closer short strike = more credit, **more chance price tags it**, higher short-put delta

| Spread | Short strike | Spot ~$94 | Cushion | Feel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **90/85** | **$90** | $94 → $90 | ~$4 (~5%) | Tighter — HOOD doesn’t need a crash to stress you |
| **85/80** | **$85** | $94 → $85 | ~$9 (~10%) | More room — needs a real selloff |

So: **short strike = the put you sold = the price level you’re betting against.**  
Risk isn’t “unlimited”; it’s **capped**, but the short strike decides how soon that risk wakes up.

## 1355. assistant

Robinhood’s **−195%** is measuring the wrong thing for risk.

### What −195% actually means

You sold the spread and collected **$200** total credit (\$1.00 × 2 contracts × 100).

To close now costs about **\$590**.

Loss so far:
\[
\$590 - \$200 = \$390
\]

As a % of the *credit*:
\[
\$390 / \$200 = 195\%
\]

So “−195%” only means: *you’ve already lost almost 2× the premium you collected.*  
It does **not** mean you’ve lost 195% of your account, or that you’re near the worst case.

---

### The real risk unit is max loss (~\$1,800)

On a **\$10-wide** put credit (400/390):

| | Per contract | ×2 |
|---|---|---|
| Width | \$10 | — |
| Credit | \$1 | \$200 |
| **Max loss** | \$10 − \$1 = **\$9** → **\$900** | **\$1,800** |

That **\$1,800** is the most you can lose if UNH is at/below \$390 at expiry (or you close at max).

You’ve lost **\$390** of that **\$1,800** so far — about **22% of max loss**, not “almost wiped out.”

---

### Why “wait because −195% feels huge” is backwards

People see **−195%** and think: *I’ve lost so much already, I have to wait for it to come back.*

That’s anchoring on the **tiny credit (\$200)**, not on the **big risk (\$1,800)**.

| Framing | Number | Feeling | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| % of credit | −195% | “Disaster — must wait” | Inflates the loss vs a small denominator |
| \$ P&L | −\$390 | Clear | Good |
| % of max loss | −\$390 / \$1,800 ≈ **22%** | “Hurt, not done” | Shows you still have **~\$1,410** of pain left |

Waiting doesn’t recover the −195%. Waiting only makes sense if you believe UNH stays **above \$400** through Aug 21. If it doesn’t, you can go from −\$390 toward −\$1,800.

---

### Simple analogy

You insured a house for a **\$200** premium with **\$1,800** of possible claim.

A claim starts: you’ve paid **\$390** so far.  
Saying “I’ve already lost 195% of my premium, so I won’t settle” ignores that the claim can still climb to **\$1,800**.

**Credit = what you were paid to take the risk.  
Max loss = the risk. Manage against max loss (and the short strike), not against % of credit.**

## 1412. assistant

Two different ideas — timing and where the short strike sits.

### 1. “Selling into a +4% rip — better on a pullback to $54–55”

A put credit spread **wins if HPE stays above your short strike**. You get paid more (fatter premium) when the market is **scared** — stock soft, IV up, puts expensive.

Today HPE is **ripping** (~+$2 from yesterday). That means:
- Puts got **cheaper** (same strike pays you less)
- You’re selling after strength has already happened — classic **chase**
- If it mean-reverts tomorrow, you still keep the credit, but you **left money on the table** vs selling when it was $54–55

**Pullback to $54–55** = stock cools off a bit, fear/IV often ticks up, **same** 52.5/47.5 (or 50/45) usually **bids higher**. Same trade, better price, and you’re not leaning into a green candle.

Analogy: don’t sell “house insurance” the day after the neighborhood had a party and everyone feels safe — wait until someone hears a noise.

---

### 2. “Income on momentum, not a clean Three Good support sell”

**Three Good** wants the short put **under a level the stock rarely closes below** (10-week support floor). For HPE that floor is roughly the **low $40s** (~$43), not $52.50.

| Style | Short strike | What you’re betting |
|---|---|---|
| **Three Good** | Near/below ~$43–45 | “It almost never dies through multi-week support” |
| **What we’re doing** | **$52.50** with spot ~$57 | “This **uptrend / rip** keeps working for 2 weeks” |

So:
- **Momentum income** = get paid because the stock is strong *right now*; short strike is only ~7% under price. A normal pullback can tag it.
- **Three Good** = get paid for sitting under a **structural floor**; much wider cushion, usually fatter relative to how “safe” it feels.

Neither is “wrong.” They’re different trades. Calling it out means: don’t treat this HPE ticket like a high-probability support sell — it’s a **short-dated bullish bet with a defined-risk coupon**, and the coupon isn’t even that fat vs width (~18%).

**One line:** rip = worse premium + chase; Three Good = short under the real floor — this short is under the *current price*, not under the *chart floor*.

## 1556. assistant

We are **not** betting that BJ goes up. We are writing a **two-sided Friday ticket** so that, if BJ’s print actually holds a direction in the first 15–30 minutes, we already know the strikes, the size, and the max we will pay.

Live now (~11:32 ET): BJ **$90.54 (−1.4%)**, WMT **$103.48 (−9.5%)**, COST **$941 (−1.6%)**. Pre-print 90/95 call debit still ~**$2.07**.

**What Friday actually is**

BJ’s Wholesale Club reports **before the open** Friday. Street is **$1.19** EPS. The stock will gap on that print the way WMT did this morning. That gap is the event. We do not sell puts through it. We do not buy the stock tonight.

**Why BJ, not COST**

WMT already dumped **~9%** on a comps/guidance miss. Warehouse clubs are the mapped read-through. The rule is: if a bellwether moves **≥5% today** *and a peer has a **new** event tomorrow*, arm the peer. BJ prints Friday. COST does **not**. Buying COST because WMT fell is the 6/26 SNDK path — chasing today’s move with no new catalyst.

**What “arm tonight” means**

Tonight we only **stage** the card. No order hits the market Thursday. At **7:00 AM PT** we recap after the number: new spot, new first-30 range, and whether 90/95 is still the right 5-wide. Then we wait for **Friday 9:30–10:00 ET**. If that opening range **holds**, we buy **1×** the debit. If it chops or fades, we stand down. Same miss as DE/WMT this morning if we show up at 11:30 instead.

**The two structures**

| If Friday’s first 30… | Buy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Holds the **high** side of the gap (rip or hold-up) | Sep 18 **90/95 call debit**, cap **$2.50** | Defined-risk long. Max loss is what we pay, ~$205–$250. |
| Holds the **low** side (dump like WMT) | Sep 18 **90/85 put debit**, same cap | The WMT-style ticket. Today’s WMT *call* card was the wrong side of a dump. |

Pre-print 90/95 is ~$2.07, under the $2.50 cap. After a gap those marks will change. If the debit is over $2.50, we **do not** chase it.

**“Flatten Friday”**

This is a **same-day** trade. Close it Friday, before the weekend. Catalyst-day moves often give back the next session. It is not a hold into next week, and it is not a new credit.

**What we are expecting, in one line**

WMT already told the consumer story. BJ will **print a number into that story**. We want a tiny, pre-written debit on whichever side the first 30 minutes actually holds — and we want to be done by Friday’s close.

This is a **defined-risk 1× debit**, not a lottery. Hard box is **about $205–$250 down vs about $250–$295 up**. Same-session you will almost never get the full $5 width. **Skip is $0** — that is part of the reward.

Live as of ~10:34 AM PT Thu: BJ **$90.50** (Wed close **$91.79**). WMT still **−8.9%** at **$104.17**. Street **$1.19**, call **8:00 AM ET** Friday. **Margin only** — agentic cash cannot buy a spread.

---

**The dollar box (1× Sep 18 5-wide, cap $2.50)**

| | Rip → **90/95 calls** | Dump → **90/85 puts** |
|---|---|---|
| Live mid debit | **$2.05** ($205) | **$2.00** ($200) |
| Natural (pay ask / hit bid) | **$2.40** ($240) | **$2.35** ($235) |
| Cap → skip if over | **$2.50** ($250) | **$2.50** ($250) |
| Max value | $5.00 | $5.00 |
| Max profit if filled at mid | **$2.95** ($295) | **$3.00** ($300) |
| Expiry R:R at mid | **1.4 : 1** | **1.5 : 1** |
| Expiry breakeven | **$92.05** | **$88.00** |
| Maxed when BJ | **≥ $95** | **≤ $85** |

Pay the cap and R:R goes to **1 : 1** ($250 risk, $250 max). That is why **$2.50 is a skip, not a “pay up.”**

---

**What the market is already pricing**

Friday weekly **$90 straddle** mid **$5.83** → implied move about **±6.4%** (**~$84.70–$96.30**). The placeholder short strikes (**$95 / $85**) sit on those wings. A **full** implied move *can* max the 5-wide. A **WMT-size −9%** to ~$82 **maxes 90/85 in the gap** — then the live debit is ~$4–$5, **over cap**, and you **recap a new 5-wide around post-print spot** (example: 85/80 or 80/75), still cap **$2.50**. Yesterday’s 90/85 is then dead. That is the recap step, not a failure of the clock.

---

**Same-session P&L (the real ticket — flatten Friday)**

You are **not** holding to Sep 18. Treat expiry max as a ceiling.

| Friday path | Likely result |
|---|---|
| Hold + continuation **~3–5%** after 7:00 AM PT | Debit **$2.05 → ~$3.00–$4.00** → **+$95 to +$195** |
| Hold + full implied wing (**~$95 or ~$85**) | Spread marks **~$3.50–$4.80** → **+$145 to +$275** |
| First 30 **chops** the range / fades VWAP | Flatten **−$50 to −$200** (most or all of the debit) |
| Debit **> $2.50**, or no hold at 7:00 AM PT | **$0**. That is a win vs DE/WMT chase |
| Wrong side, don’t flatten | Full **−$205 to −$250** |

Delta of the live 90/95 is only **~0.20**. A $1 BJ move is ~$20 on the spread. The money is **intrinsic after a real gap**, not tick-chasing.

---

**Risks that are not in the $250**

1. **Clock.** Fire at **~7:00 AM PT**. After that you are the DE/WMT chase. Process loss = buying a dead debit for $250.
2. **WMT-style print.** EPS beat + comps/guide miss → dump. Recap the **side** from comps/guidance, not from EPS vs $1.19 alone.
3. **Already-maxed spread.** A −9% open makes 90/85 un-buyable under the cap. Recap or stand down. Do not “just pay $4.”
4. **Fill quality.** Sep **90C OI 24**, **95C OI 39**. The 90C market is **$4.10–$4.50**. Slippage can eat **$20–$40** of a $205 debit. Puts are better (**90P OI 593**).
5. **IV crush.** You buy **after** the print. Sep 18 is there so theta does not kill you the same day; it does **not** replace a hold. Chop still loses.
6. **Do not stack ROST** if BJ fills. One catalyst debit.

---

**One-line summary**

**Risk: $0 if you skip, ~$205–$250 if you fire. Reward: ~$100–$200 typical same-day if it holds, ~$250–$295 only if the wing is hit. After 7:00 AM PT the reward is not on the table.**
